scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] The Glessner Household.

[short pause] A spring morning... April 1904, at 1800 Prairie Avenue. On every other walk the people are out of your way. [short pause] This time... they are the walk.

Seven stops round the outside of the house, and at each one somebody who lives or works here is waiting at their own door: John and Frances Glessner, their cook, the parlor maid and the house maid, the stable helper, and the old coachman, who left the Glessners in 1902 and has come back this morning to show you his stable. [amused] Each tells you what they do here, and sends you on to the next.

[thoughtful] The people and the facts are from the house's own records: John Glessner's 1923 account of the house, the museum's research into Frances Glessner's journals, and the census of 1900. The words they say are written for this walk.

[short pause] [warmly] Mr. Glessner is on his front walk. Go and say good morning.
scripts.stop:john: [warmly] Good morning, and welcome to 1800 Prairie Avenue. I'm John Glessner. I came to Chicago from Springfield, Ohio, in 1870... a few weeks married, to be nearer the farmers who buy our machines. [proudly] We sold 800 of them in 1871 — and 25,000 in 1884. And two years ago our firm went into the new International Harvester Company. Mr. Richardson designed this house, his last work, and we slept here first on 1 December 1887. [chuckles] A dear old lady once said to me, 'you get it from your wife and your house', meaning my place in this town. [short pause] I took it as a compliment... for I selected the one, and I built the other. Everyone who keeps the house is about this morning. Mrs. Glessner is in the courtyard: go in under the house by the carriage passage, just to your left.
scripts.stop:frances: [delighted] You found us! I'm Frances Glessner. Out here the house shows its sunny face: see the rounded bay of the hall, and the door whose yellow glass makes the hall feel sunny... even on a grey Chicago day. The creeper on these walls came from our old house — one vine fifty-five feet long — and it flourished. Every Monday morning through the winter and spring my Reading Class meets in the library, the ladies sewing while we read. [proudly] This year I have set up a silversmith's bench in the basement, [laughs softly] and I keep bees. I have kept a journal since 1879, and in it I write down every servant we hire, their pay, and why they left. [sighs] One August evening in 1891, all five of our staff handed in their notice... after dinner. [short pause] So I sent for Mattie. Go and meet her by the kitchen side of the court.
scripts.stop:mattie: [cheerfully] Hello! Mattie Williamson, the cook. This house keeps one cook: [laughs] me. I was born in Quebec, and my brother Alex runs the Glessners' farm in New Hampshire; each summer I go a week ahead of the family to open the house. In the winter of 1891 Mrs. Glessner went through seven cooks in seven weeks... all beaten by her new gas stove! And in February 1892 she wrote, [primly] 'Mattie Williamson is going to try my cooking. I shall have her taught.' [chuckles] My kitchen is through this wall; a board of bells tells us which room is calling. I send up eight-course dinners and feed the staff besides; we eat our own dinner at three, so the kitchen is clear for the family's. [excited] In January last year the whole orchestra came to dinner... and played Beethoven on my pots and pans! [laughs] Christine is back from market, round at the corner.
scripts.stop:christine: [brightly] Hej! Christine Nelson, the parlor maid. I came over from Sweden in 1892. Mattie and the waitress feed the house, and the ladies' maid looks after the ladies' clothes; the cleaning is mine... [sighs] and in this city that never ends. The smoke is so thick the drawings in the hall had to go under glass. [amused] People walking by laugh at those narrow windows along Eighteenth Street. They only light the corridors, and those corridors are ours: every room has two doors or more, and the passages are planned so that servants rarely are in evidence. [proudly] You can clean a whole floor and never cross the family. [chuckles] Even the iceman stays out: he pushes the ice through a little half-door into the cold closet. Mary keeps the rooms with me. She'll be at our door under the great arch.
scripts.stop:mary: [warmly] Hello, I'm Mary Reynolds, the house maid, and an Illinois girl. Welcome to our side of the house! Under the great arch is our own front door. [proudly] We even have our own address, 35 Eighteenth Street, so our letters never mix with the family's. We women sleep up above the kitchen wing, four bedrooms off one hall, with a little porch over the street. The men live over the coach house, and there is no way through from their wing to ours. [mischievously] This door is also where the music gets smuggled in. [whispers] On the twenty-fifth wedding anniversary, Mr. Thomas brought the entire orchestra in this way and up the back stairs... and nobody upstairs knew a thing until they began to play! [laughs] On New Year's Day last year a double quartet of horns crept up the same way. Charles, our coachman until 1902, is back at the stable doors.
scripts.stop:charles: [warmly] Good morning to you. Charles Nelson. [chuckles] I'll be honest with you: I'm not the coachman here in 1904. I drove for Mr. Glessner from 1878, back at the old house on Washington Street, until 1902... and I've come back this morning to show you my old stable. I came from Sweden in 1871, and by 1900 Martha and I had five children in the rear building here. [proudly] Six stalls, and room in the carriage house for as many carriages, all white glazed brick so it can be washed down like a dairy. The furnace room is underneath, so coal and ashes never come near the house. [fondly] When they broke ground in June 1886, young George drove his father's horse and buggy to the site, and threw the first soil with his sister. [short pause] Who holds the reins now... the records don't say. August is round the corner at the courtyard gates.
scripts.stop:august: [cheerfully] Hallo! August Billings, the stable helper. I came over from Sweden in 1892, same year as Christine, and I sleep in the rear building with the other men. The coachman has me at the harness and washing down the carriage, and I see to the doves too: [proudly] the dovecotes hold near sixty, and their eggs go to the family's table. These gates are the back way into the court. [softly] They tell a story about them from before my time. In December 1887 the family brought every stick they owned in through here and into the house... before the neighbours suspected even that they were about to move! [chuckles] That night they lit the new hearth with fire carried from the old one. [warmly] That's the whole household. Thank you for coming round!
scripts.ending:finish: [thoughtful] Two years after this morning, in 1906, the Glessners gave up horses for motor cars, and the wall between the stable and the carriage house came down. [short pause] Mattie cooked here until 1912, when she left to marry in California; Frances Glessner wrote of her that she was 'one of the finest people that ever lived.' [short pause] John and Frances lived in this house to the end of their lives, and in 1924 he signed a deed of gift for it. [softly] The rooms these people kept... are a museum now.
